paras: The threatened lynching of Charles Rigney took place at Rockville, Maryland, in November 1881, after Rigney, a young Black farm hand, was accused of assaulting the five-year-old daughter of a Montrose storekeeper. The girl's father beat him and, with four other men, bound him and delivered him to the county jail, and threats to take him out and lynch him were reported for two nights. No attack came; the grand jury indicted him for an attempt rather than rape, and papers reported that the danger of lynching had passed.

Montrose was a small settlement on the turnpike between Rockville and Washington, where Charles Lochte kept a store. Rigney, who said he was nineteen, worked on a nearby farm and was accused of luring the child into a barn or stable, by the Sentinel's account with an offer of twenty-five cents. Both Rockville reporters recalled Diggs, "the colored ravisher" hanged on a tree about a year earlier.

The alleged assault took place on the afternoon of Saturday, November 19. According to the Star's Rockville correspondent, Lochte followed Rigney's tracks into the woods and would have killed him had his helpers not stopped him, whereas the local Sentinel said Lochte called Rigney out of the store and thrashed him until "cooler heads" in the crowd interfered. When the Star's correspondent saw Rigney in jail he had a bruised eye and swollen nose from the beating, and he denied the charge.

Lochte and four other men tied Rigney with rope and drove him by wagon from Montrose to Rockville, where he was surrendered to Sheriff Kelchener and held by Jailor Kingsbury. Only the Star reported that one of the five tied a rope around Rigney's neck on the way and led him by it from the wagon, adding that "it is said" a lynching was averted only because two of the men had drunk too much cider. The Sentinel instead said he was taken before Justice Morgan, who committed him for the grand jury.

Talk of lynching was heard on Saturday night and again on Sunday, but nothing was done, and a Sunday-night dispatch described Rockville as quiet, with the sheriff gone to bed. On Monday the Star reported a party organizing at Montrose and a lynching expected if the grand jury indicted for rape, though the sheriff expected no attack that night.

By a Rockville dispatch of November 22 the grand jury had indicted Rigney for an attempt at outrage, and the child was reported less injured than first thought. The Baltimore Sun's correspondent wrote that the chances of lynching had "about passed away" and that the law would take its course, and a Baltimore German paper likewise reported that Rockville no longer feared a lynching. No one was reported arrested for the beating or the threats, and no report of a trial or sentence was found.

Washington papers carried the story on Monday, November 21, the Evening Star under the headlines "NEGRO OUTRAGE ON A LITTLE GIRL" and "THREATS OF LYNCHING," the Critic as "A Candidate for Lynch Law," and the National Republican as "A Candidate for Hemp." The Star's correspondent called Rigney "the fiend" and "the ravisher" and wrote that a lynching would "save the state expense, as the law hangs all convicted for rape." The same day a Rockville wire ran in Wilmington's Daily Gazette and the Baltimore German-language Deutsche Correspondent called Rigney a "Neger" and the child Lochte's white daughter.

The Rockville Sentinel, the local weekly, used the slur "darky" and urged a penitentiary term of eight or ten years, while warning that for such crimes "a terrible ultimatum" was held in reserve. Later a Baltimore Sun paragraph in Charles Town, West Virginia, reported "another colored man" charged with outraging "a white girl," and Jackson's Weekly Clarion reprinted two sentences of the first dispatch.

The two Rockville accounts differ on where Rigney was caught and beaten, on whether he went straight to the sheriff or first before a justice, and on the rope around his neck, which the Sentinel does not mention. Early reports called the assault brutal, but later ones, including the attending physician as quoted by the Sentinel, said the child's injuries were not serious.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Charles Rigney
bases: A white man and his helpers beat, bound and roped a Black man accused of assaulting a child, and papers reported repeated threats to take him from the Rockville jail and lynch him, none carried out (A1, A2, A3, A8).

Rigney was not killed; he was indicted and the lynching threats, made in the name of punishing an alleged rape, were reported to have passed away (A1, A7, A6). The size of any party that meant to take him from jail is not given; the only group with a number is the five captors (A1).

The Star's correspondent, a Republican special, a Rockville wire, a Baltimore German paper and the local Sentinel independently agree on the capture, beating and talk of lynching (A1, A2, A4, A5, A8); the rope round the neck appears only in A1.

accounts.label: Star correspondent at Rockville
accounts.gist: Lochte tracked Rigney into the woods and would have killed him but for his helpers; the five bound him, one tied a rope round his neck, and a lynching on the road was said to have been averted only because two had drunk cider; threats continued and a lynching was expected if the indictment was for rape.

accounts.label: Rockville wire and Republican special
accounts.gist: The father caught Rigney leaving the barn and would have killed him had others not protected him; there was talk of lynching two nights running, but nothing was done and Rockville was quiet.

accounts.label: Montgomery County Sentinel (local)
accounts.gist: Lochte called Rigney out of his store, accused and thrashed him until the crowd interfered; he was bound, taken before Justice Morgan and committed; the girl's injuries were not serious.

accounts.label: Baltimore Sun special
accounts.gist: The grand jury indicted for attempt only, the child was less hurt than first thought, and the chances of lynching had passed; an indictment for the full offence would have meant a lynching.

framing.detail: The Evening Star headlined 'NEGRO OUTRAGE ON A LITTLE GIRL' and 'THREATS OF LYNCHING', called Rigney 'the fiend' and 'the ravisher', and said a lynching 'will save the state expense'.
The Critic and Republican ran the same short special under 'A Candidate for Lynch Law' and 'A Candidate for Hemp', calling him 'the fiend' but reporting the quiet night without comment.

The Rockville Sentinel urged a penitentiary term of eight or ten years and enforcement of the law, but warned of 'a terrible ultimatum held in reserve' and closed with a joke about 'Out west' lynching.

The Wilmington Gazette and Jackson's Weekly Clarion reprinted the Rockville dispatches; the Spirit of Jefferson ran a Baltimore Sun paragraph calling him 'another colored man' charged with outraging 'a white girl'.

He was never taken from custody: captured after a pursuit by the father and four men and delivered to the sheriff; the threatened jail lynching did not happen.
Pursuit, beating, binding, a rope round the neck, threats; no hanging.
Charles Lochte and four other men (the captors); those threatening lynching unnamed.
1: bruised eye and swollen nose from Lochte's beating.
The violence done was by the father and his four helpers; a mob is only threatened, never reported assembling.

info: Alleged assault and capture on Saturday, November 19, 1881 (Saturday afternoon); threats of lynching Saturday night and Sunday night, November 19-20.
Alleged assault in a barn or stable at Montrose, a settlement on the turnpike from Rockville toward Washington/Georgetown; Rigney held in the jail at Rockville, where the lynching threats were aimed.
Charles Rigney, described as a 'negro farm hand' (A1), 'colored man' who worked on an adjoining farm (A2), 'colored lad' (A8); he said he was nineteen (A1, A8); the German paper gives twenty (A5).

Accused of assaulting ('outraging') the five-year-old daughter of Montrose storekeeper Charles Lochte after luring her into a barn or stable; he denied it (A1). Indicted for attempt at outrage / attempted rape.

Charles Lochte, the girl's father, beat him; Lochte and four other men bound him and drove him to Rockville, and one of the five tied a rope round his neck. Those who threatened lynching are unnamed; a party was reported organizing at Montrose.
Not lynched; reports said the chances of lynching had 'about passed away' and the law would take its course. No report of a trial or sentence was found.
